newsitem.title: USA: GM faces production losses in Oklahoma strike.
newsitem.headline: GM faces production losses in Oklahoma strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. faced its first production losses Monday from a strike at its Oklahoma City car plant as bargainers met Sunday in an effort to resolve the disute.

Rick Jones, a spokesman for United Auto Workers Local 1999, said negotiations centering on staffing levels resumed at about 11 a.m. EDT Sunday, but there was no indication of any progress toward a settlement.
About 3,500 UAW workers struck the plant at 12:59 a.m. EST Saturday after a deadline for reaching a new local labor agreement expired. Bargainers met for several hours later Saturday with no result.
The walkout will prevent GM from resuming production of its new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars at the plant, which GM's main production source for the cars.

Because the Oklahoma City plant is a final assembly operation, a prolonged walkout is not expected to have a widespread effect on GM's North American operations, as a strike at a key parts plant would. But the strike could force plants that supply parts to Oklahoma City, including those owned by GM and some outside suppliers, to curtail production.
The Oklahoma walkout is the latest of several local strikes that GM has been hit with or threatened with since it signed a new national labor contract with the UAW last November.

Although the national pact required GM to maintain employment levels equal to 95 of its 215,000-member UAW workforce, it allows GM to shrink through retirement attrition at plants where it installs new, more efficient technology.

GM is trying to do just that at Oklahoma City, where it says it needs 900 fewer workers to build the Malibu and Cutlass than it needed to build previous models. GM contends that the UAW agreed to "competitive staffing levels" to help persuade the automaker to build the new cars in Oklahoma City.
But the union, whose members say they are overworked with growing numbers of injuries, wants GM to replace 500 workers lost to retirements and transfers to other plants in recent months.
The Malibu and Cutlass, priced at about $16,000 to $18,000, are a cornerstone of GM's efforts to regain market share in the hotly contested U.S. intermediate car segment, which it once dominated.
GM this week reported stronger-than-expected March U.S. sales of the Malibu, which increased to 12,260 cars from 5,800 in February.

The 18-year-old Oklahoma City plant, which has never before had a strike had a strike, is up to about 80 percent of its full production capacity. A second plant, in Wilmington, Del., just began production of Malibus about two weeks ago, but is much further behind on its launch curve.
